title: NumPy Array vs Python List
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Step through doubling five numbers to see why a Python list of scattered objects is processed one element at a time while a NumPy array is one block of values handled in a single call.

educational.topic: How Python lists and NumPy arrays store data
learningObjectives: Students will be able to explain how a Python list and a NumPy array store the same numbers and why that difference makes whole-array NumPy operations use less memory and run faster.
prerequisites: Creating a NumPy array with np.array

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side-by-side step-through of a worked example, with prediction before the first step
keyQuestions: What does a Python list actually store in its slots?
Why can NumPy skip the type check that Python does for every list element?
Why are the addresses of the array values exactly 8 apart?
When would a NumPy array not be faster than a list?
commonMisconceptions: A Python list stores its numbers side by side (it stores pointers, and the numbers are separate objects).
NumPy is fast because it does less arithmetic (it does the same arithmetic, but in compiled code with no per-element overhead).
NumPy is always faster (on a handful of elements the fixed cost of the call can make it slower than a list).
assessmentOpportunities: Students draw their own picture of the list `[10, 20, 30]` and the array `np.array([10, 20, 30])` in memory and write two sentences explaining why `arr * 2` is faster than `[x * 2 for x in nums]` on a large array, and why the gain disappears on a tiny one.
